props.title: House of Usher

sections.content: Roger Corman's House of Usher launched American International Pictures' celebrated Poe cycle, establishing a new standard for Gothic horror. Vincent Price delivers a mesmerizing performance as Roderick Usher, capturing the character's aristocratic decay and hypersensitive nature. The film's saturated colors and atmospheric cinematography by Floyd Crosby created a template that influenced Gothic cinema for decades, notably visible in Dario Argento's Suspiria (1977) and Guillermo del Toro's Crimson Peak (2015).

sections.content: The success of House of Usher sparked a Gothic horror renaissance in the 1960s. Hammer Films responded with increasingly colorful productions like The Curse of Frankenstein (1957) and Horror of Dracula (1958), while Italian directors like Mario Bava created Black Sunday (1960) and Kill, Baby... Kill! (1966). These films shared Usher's emphasis on atmosphere over shock, using color cinematography to create dreamlike supernatural environments.

The film's influence extends beyond pure horror. Its themes of aristocratic decline and familial curse echo through Stanley Kubrick's The Shining (1980) and Peter Medak's The Changeling (1980). The way Corman uses architecture as a character - the house itself representing the Usher family's mental state - created a blueprint for haunted house films like Robert Wise's The Haunting (1963) and James Wan's The Conjuring (2013). sections.content: Corman's use of the mansion as a psychological metaphor revolutionized horror cinema's approach to setting. The house's gradual destruction parallels Roderick's mental deterioration, a technique later employed in Robert Wise's The Haunting (1963) and Alejandro Amenábar's The Others (2001). This architectural symbolism influenced everything from Dan Curtis's Dark Shadows (1966-1971) to Guillermo del Toro's Crimson Peak (2015).
